Rapid growth

The Shale Boom

Cheap gas looks like an opportunity. A power plant is a long commitment to a fuel price that can change much faster.

Location

Your term

The situation

Your starting point

You begin in 2006 with a coal plant and a decision about what comes next. The shale boom makes natural gas increasingly attractive as your utility grows.

A low fuel bill today does not guarantee one for the life of a new plant. This twenty-year scenario gives your investment time to pay off, and gives fuel prices time to test the assumptions behind it.

The choices

What will you do?

  1. 01

    Choose how far to lean into gas

    Compare the immediate savings with the cost of tying more of your fleet to a single fuel.

  2. 02

    Prepare for a less comfortable year

    Leave room for price shocks and reduced output. A plan built around the cheapest months may struggle when conditions change.

  3. 03

    Grow without losing your footing

    Match construction to demand and keep enough cash to operate. Cheap generation does little good if the company cannot finance its next move.

Put your plan to the test

How much of a temporary advantage would you turn into a twenty-year investment?

Build, watch what happens, and try a different approach. The grid is yours to run.
